1408.title: Sh-A-L
1408.hook: sha'al, to ask; she'elah, a question
1408.howItsDone: At the Passover seder the youngest child traditionally asks why this night is different, and Jews bring hard questions of practice to a rabbi; the written exchanges are called she'elot u'teshuvot, questions and answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-Ch-D: echad, one, the Shema's last word. Your line was one. A new week starts with a question, and the seder's four children, from day six hundred seventy-nine, come back.

A woman named Hannah is praying in the sanctuary at Shiloh, so hard that her lips move but no sound comes out, and the priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't. She's asking for a child. In time she has a son, and the text gives her own explanation of his name: she "called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the LORD." Asked is she'iltiv, from the root sha'al. The prophet's whole life starts as an answer to someone's question.
screen: `HANNAH PRAYS WITHOUT A SOUND.` → `A SON NAMED SAMUEL.` → `I HAVE ASKED HIM OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Sh-A-L. Shin, alef, lamed. Sha'al: to ask. She'elah: a question. First, asking after someone. Joseph, now a ruler in Egypt, sees his brothers again, and they don't yet know who he is. When they bow to him, the text says: "he asked them of their welfare." In Hebrew, he asked them for shalom, and then about their old father. Here asking isn't only for information. It's how you reach for someone. Second, the table. The Torah expects children to ask: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The Passover seder is built around that. The youngest asks why this night is different. The Haggadah imagines four kinds of children, and one of them doesn't know how to ask at all. For that child, it says, you open the conversation yourself. A question is so central that if it's missing, someone has to start one. Third, the library. For centuries, when Jews had a hard question about how to live, they wrote to a rabbi, and the rabbi wrote back. Those letters are called she'elot u'teshuvot: questions and answers. Whole shelves of Jewish law grew out of people asking. In this tradition, a question isn't a sign you're lost. It's how the conversation stays alive.

Let one simple question take shape, the way Joseph asked after his brothers' shalom, and hold it quietly, the way Hannah held hers, lips barely moving. If you pray, you can pray for that person's shalom too.

1409.title: A-N-H
1409.hook: anah, to answer, and ani, the poor or humble
1409.howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching prizes anavah, humility, and holds up Moses as its model from Numbers 12:3; Proverbs' 'soft answer' is a common Jewish guide for replying in a quarrel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-A-L: sha'al, to ask, Hannah's asking and the child who can't ask yet. Your line was ask. Humility had its own day, back on day one thousand two hundred fifty-six; today, the root under it.

Someone snaps at you. A text in capitals, a remark across the table, a customer who's had a long day and decided you're the reason. You have about one second before you answer. Proverbs has a line for that second: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." The Hebrew for answer there is ma'aneh, from the root ayin, nun, hey. Read those letters another way, and they give a word for someone poor, low, bowed down. An answer, and a humble person.
screen: `SOMEONE SNAPS AT YOU.` → `A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.` → `THE SAME LETTERS: THE LOWLY.`

segments.voice: A-N-H. Ayin, nun, hey. First, to answer: anah, the everyday verb for replying, and also for God answering. A psalm says: "This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him." The word for poor there is ani, written with the same letters. It isn't the ani that means I; that one starts with a different letter, alef. This ani is the lowly one, with nothing to bargain with. And the psalm says that one is heard. Second, humility. From the same letters comes anav, humble, and anavah, humility. The Torah uses it for Moses, of all people, the leader who spoke with God: "Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth." Meek there is anav. The text doesn't call him the smartest or the strongest. It calls him the humblest. Third, the honest part. Dictionaries often list answering and being lowly as two separate roots that share letters; whether they were ever one word is a question for linguists. So the link isn't a hidden code. But some readers hear them together, and the pairing teaches something: the soft answer is the humble answer. It doesn't need to win, or arrive with a speech prepared. It answers the way Moses led, from low down. And the psalm adds the other side: the one who is low is the one whose cry gets answered.

Let it sit for a breath, then look for a lower one that leaves room for the other person, maybe starting with you might be right, or tell me more. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer.

1410.title: N-D-V
1410.howItsDone: Alongside obligatory tzedakah, Jewish tradition honors the nedavah, a gift given of one's own accord; the wilderness sanctuary in Exodus was built from such freewill offerings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-N-H: the soft answer, the poor one who is heard, and Moses, very meek. Your line was answer humbly. Today, a gift nobody can require.

Here is a fundraiser that had to be shut down for raising too much. The people in the wilderness are building the mishkan, the sanctuary, and they keep bringing gold, silver, yarn, linen, wood, every morning, more. Finally the craftsmen go to Moses and say: "The people bring much more than enough." So Moses has it announced through the camp: stop. And the scene ends with a line that's almost funny: "So the people were restrained from bringing." Restrained. From giving.
screen: `BUILDING THE SANCTUARY.` → `MUCH MORE THAN ENOUGH.` → `RESTRAINED FROM BRINGING.`

segments.voice: N-D-V. Nun, dalet, vet. Nedavah: a freewill gift, a voluntary offering. The verb: to give of your own accord, to volunteer. First, the instruction. When God asks for gifts for the sanctuary, the request is left open: "of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering." The gift is measured by the heart that moves it, not the size. And the text calls what they bring a nedavah, from men and women whose hearts made them willing. Second, the person. From the same letters comes nadiv: a generous person, and also a noble one. Isaiah says: "the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand." In that old English, liberal means generous, and the Hebrew is nadiv. Notice the verb: deviseth. The generous person plans generosity, thinks it up, the way someone else plans a business. Third, the difference. Jewish law also has required giving. Tzedakah, the giving to the poor, is commanded; the Torah's tithes are counted. A nedavah is the gift nobody can require. Both matter, and neither replaces the other. But the nedavah has its own shine: the people heard the request and simply kept coming, until someone had to ask them to stop. A free gift isn't free because it costs nothing. It's free because nobody made you.

1411.title: N-D-R
1411.howItsDone: Some Jews add bli neder, 'without a vow', to everyday promises so they won't become binding vows, and the evening service of Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, a formula about the release of vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-D-V: nedavah, the freewill gift, so generous Moses had to ask the people to stop. Your line was free gift. Kol Nidre had its own day, back on day six hundred fifty-three. Today, change one letter, and the gift becomes a promise.

"I'll bring the dessert on Friday, bli neder." Listen around some Jewish tables and you'll hear those two words tacked onto ordinary promises. Bli neder: without a vow. It sounds like a hedge, a way of getting out of the cake. It's the opposite. It comes from taking a vow so seriously that you don't want a casual promise about dessert to become one by accident.
screen: `I'LL BRING DESSERT, BLI NEDER.` → `WITHOUT A VOW.` → `NOT A HEDGE: RESPECT.`

segments.voice: N-D-R. Nun, dalet, resh. Neder: a vow, a promise made before God. First, the weight of a word. The Torah says that when someone vows a vow, "he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." What comes out of your mouth becomes something you owe. Second, the advice. Ecclesiastes, Kohelet, the Gatherer from a few days ago, says it plainly: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Not a ban on vows. A warning about making them cheap. That's where bli neder comes from: a habit of guarding the word. Third, the night the vows are spoken about. Yom Kippur evening opens with Kol Nidre, all vows, from this root: a legal formula, sung slowly, that asks for release from vows a person can't keep. It's been argued over and explained in more than one way. Some read it as a mercy for the person who promised too much. Some hear a whole community admitting how often words outrun lives. Either way, Yom Kippur night begins not with a hymn but with the subject of promises. And yesterday's word is the neighbor here. The rabbis set the two side by side: a nedavah is a gift you hand over, a neder is a promise you take on. One letter apart, and both start with a willing heart. But a vow follows you out the door.

1412.title: B-T-Ch
1412.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on bitachon, trust in God, runs from Proverbs and the Psalms to the gate of trust in Bachya ibn Pakuda's Duties of the Heart; some Jews repeat Nachum Ish Gamzu's words, gam zu l'tovah, this too is for the good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-D-R: neder, a vow. Your line was vow. Bitachon had a first, gentle day back on day one thousand two hundred sixty-three. Today, the root underneath it, and under any promise someone else makes to you.

A man in the Talmud goes by Nachum Ish Gamzu, and his nickname is a sentence. Whatever happened to him, he would say gam zu l'tovah: this too is for the good. Once, the story goes, he was sent to the emperor with a chest of jewels as a gift. At an inn on the way, the chest was emptied in the night and filled with dirt. He arrived, opened it before the emperor, and there was only earth. The Talmud tells how the dirt turned out to be useful after all, and he came home honored. Whatever you make of the ending, the man had a habit.
screen: `NACHUM ISH GAMZU.` → `A CHEST OF JEWELS, FULL OF DIRT.` → `THIS TOO IS FOR THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: B-T-Ch. Bet, tet, chet. Bitachon: trust. First, the verb. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." Trust is something you do, and the verse sets it against leaning on your own reading of events. Second, the same letters mean safety. Leviticus promises that if the people keep the commandments, "ye shall dwell in the land in safety." The Hebrew is la-vetach, from this root. And a psalm uses it at bedtime: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Trusting and being safe live under one roof. Trust is somewhere you can lie down. Third, a book. The Jewish philosopher Bachya ibn Pakuda wrote Duties of the Heart, and one of its gates is the gate of trust. He treats trust as work done inside, by the heart, while a person still does their part in the world. Fourth, back to Nachum. Jewish thinkers have argued about what bitachon expects. Some teach that it means confidence that things will turn out well. Others teach that it means confidence that whatever comes is held by God, even when it doesn't look good. Nachum's sentence can be heard either way. What both readings share is the moment he said it: with the dirt in front of him, before he knew how the story would end.

1413.title: Sh-B-R
1413.hook: shever, a break; mashber, a birthstool (Isaiah 37:3): breaking can bring birth
1413.howItsDone: Jewish teaching returns to the broken tablets kept in the ark beside the whole ones (Berakhot 8b) and to the psalm's promise that God is near the broken of heart; the Hebrew mashber, a birthstool in Isaiah 37:3, shares the root of shever, a break.

segments.voice: Yesterday, B-T-Ch: bitachon, trust, and betach, safety. Your line was trust. Today, what the language does with a break.

Stone tablets, carried down a mountain. Moses comes near the camp, sees the golden calf and the dancing, and in the King James words, "he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount." Later he carves a second set and carries them up again. The Talmud adds a detail the Torah doesn't spell out: the broken pieces weren't swept away. The rabbis teach that the whole tablets and the broken tablets were both placed in the ark, and carried together.
screen: `TABLETS, DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` → `BROKEN AT ITS FOOT.` → `THE PIECES WENT IN THE ARK.`

segments.voice: Sh-B-R. Shin, bet, resh. Shever: a break, a fracture. First, the heart. A psalm says, "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart." The Hebrew is nishberei lev, the broken of heart, from this root. The verse doesn't say near the whole. It says near the broken. Second, a surprise. A word from these same letters, mashber, turns up in Isaiah, when King Hezekiah sends a desperate message to the prophet: "for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth." Where the King James says the birth, the Hebrew has mashber, which readers understand as the birthstool, where a woman in labor sat. Hezekiah uses it for a crisis that has stalled. So one root holds two things: the break and the birth. Third, back to the ark. The Talmud draws a lesson about people from it: honor an elder who has forgotten their learning through no fault of their own, because the broken tablets lay in the ark too. Broken still belongs in the holiest place. Fourth, a careful word. The tradition doesn't say every break is secretly good, or that pain is a present. Hezekiah's line is a cry: there is not strength to bring forth. The root simply won't let a break be only an ending. It keeps a birthstool in the same letters.
screen: `NEAR THE BROKEN OF HEART.` · `MASHBER: THE BIRTHSTOOL.` · `THE BROKEN TABLETS STAYED.` · `A CRY, NOT A SLOGAN.` · then, large: `BREAKING CAN BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that cracked, a plan, a friendship, a body that stopped doing what it used to, a medium one, not the hardest, and hold it for a few breaths without trying to fix it. Then ask gently whether anything began there; if nothing comes, that's an honest answer too, since the broken tablets were kept anyway. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart. And if a break ever feels too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

1414.title: T-K-N
1414.hook: tikkun, to fix, to set right
1414.howItsDone: Tikkun appears in the Mishnah's court rules made 'for the setting-right of the world', in the Aleinu's hope to set the world right, and in Lurianic Kabbalah's gathering of scattered sparks; some Jews today use tikkun olam for social action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-B-R: shever, a break, and mashber, the birthstool. Your line was breaking can birth. Repairing the world had its first day back on day one thousand fifty-three; today, the root that picks up the pieces.

"That which is crooked cannot be made straight." That's Ecclesiastes, Kohelet in Hebrew, sounding tired. The verb behind made straight is today's root, and he comes back to it: "who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?" And yet near the end of the same book, the writer is remembered as someone who "set in order many proverbs," and the Hebrew uses the same verb again. A man who says crooked things can't be straightened spends his days straightening sentences.
screen: `CROOKED CANNOT BE MADE STRAIGHT.` → `WHO CAN MAKE IT STRAIGHT?` → `HE SET PROVERBS IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun. Tikkun: fixing, setting right, putting in order. First, the court. The Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce documents and freeing servants, keeps giving one reason for rules the rabbis put in place: mipnei tikkun ha-olam, for the setting-right of the world. It's practical. A rule so that a man can't quietly cancel a divorce document he has already sent, behind his wife's back, so that she believes she is free when she isn't. Tikkun olam begins as good order in a courtroom. Second, prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of services, hopes for a day l'taken olam, to set the world right under the sovereignty of the Almighty. Here the fixing is God's, and it's on the horizon. Third, the mystics. The Kabbalah of Isaac Luria tells of vessels that couldn't hold the divine light and shattered, scattering sparks. The word for that shattering is shevirah, from yesterday's root; the work of gathering the sparks is tikkun. The break comes first, and the fixing answers it. Fourth, today. Some Jews use the phrase for social action, mending the world through justice and care. Others hear the court or the prayer first. All of it lives in these letters. Kohelet may be right that some crooked things stay crooked. He still set his proverbs in order.
screen: `FOR THE SETTING-RIGHT OF THE WORLD.` · `THE ALEINU: TO SET THE WORLD RIGHT.` · `SHATTERED VESSELS, GATHERED SPARKS.` · `TODAY: MENDING THE WORLD.` · then, large: `FIX WHAT YOU CAN REACH.`

segments.voice: Walk back through your day and find one small thing left out of order: a reply you owe, a small mistake you noticed and let go, a drawer that won't close. Hold it for a few breaths and decide exactly how you'll set it right. If you pray, you can hold the Aleinu's hope in mind while you look.
screen: `FIND ONE THING OUT OF ORDER.` · `DECIDE HOW.`

segments.voice: T-K-N. Tav, kuf, nun: tikkun, setting right. And this week's lines in order: ask, answer humbly, free gift, vow, trust, breaking can birth, fix. Today's word.
Your line: fix. The one crooked thing in front of you is enough for one day. See you tomorrow.
